entries.rationale: The closed memory-only runtime specializes every applicable source obligation: immutable store/lifecycle scope, target-shaped basis identity including basis-kind, current/authoritative/at-least/exact acquisition outcomes, borrowed any-thread ownership, acquisition/release metering, idempotent close, use-after-release rejection, and construction-failure cleanup. Generic multi-backend source construction, owned native handles, and virtual-thread rejection are unreachable in this single borrowed-memory topology.

The specialized immutable-basis adapter is a constant closed three-operation read table with no caller configuration, connection, source-selection, or writer authority. Its selected-basis identity admits only ordinary/as-of views, exact integers stay within the memory order boundary, and every physical adapter callback including relationship-half certification is metered. Generic protocols, optional backend operations, and virtual/runtime profiles are not linked in the closed Jank topology.
The production Jank dispatcher is immutable and exposes no writer; initialization uses a closed local bootstrap path rather than Core's backend writer surface.
Request publication control is proven; proof-frame, managed-current, and cross-basis cache changes remain unqualified.
The file has a large source, writer, proof, continuation, and lifecycle delta beyond the verified request controls and error identities.

The native memory selector covers every applicable locked-Core outcome: current and authoritative selection, at-least satisfaction or typed failure, authenticated retained exact with no fall-forward, selected-basis token identity, store/lifecycle/expiry/future-skew rejection, pre-selection cancellation/deadline checks, and exact-once cleanup. The removed direct-adapter path and generic multi-backend source envelope are not linked by the closed memory runtime.
The Jank runtime uses closed local continuation artifacts; replay, lineage, and publication semantics require comparison.
The public function surface is intentionally specialized and has not been exhaustively mapped to the target Core API.

Every applicable target cursor change is specialized and tested: TTL-bearing encode entries are client-local and keyed by a conservative issuance bucket plus the complete payload, decode entries retain the authenticated expiry and call current-time validation on every hit, cache configuration errors carry paired identities, and all cursor producers expose the locked :eacl.pagination/invalid-cursor identity. The generic bidirectional codec maps and their stale-reverse-eviction case do not exist in the one-key local cache implementation; continuation acceptance remains tracked under the separate engine/relay entries.
The closed Jank memory engine has no service-edge physical topology or provider protocol; its width-one local scans are independently bounded.
The target change only renames current-cache stages absent from the Jank decision slice; equivalent direct local-cache behavior is executable-tested.
The sole target change adds an error identity to a callback-based relationship window not present in the closed Jank engine.
The specialized Jank pagination loops require cross-runtime ordering, boundary, and replay vectors.
The only target source change makes a helper test-visible and does not alter runtime behavior.
Plan read-scope certification is proven; remaining permission dependency, caching, and enumeration changes are unqualified.
Every exposed Jank workload limit is a positive integer capped far below 2^53-1; no generic portable host-number boundary is exposed.
This JVM-only generated-class availability error path is not executable in a native Jank custom runtime.
Generated JVM decision bindings are not linked into the native Jank runtime; equivalent result semantics remain covered under the separate engine entries.
The Jank port uses compact relation-stamp proofs and has not qualified target Core lineage and proof-frame behavior.
The sole semantic change adds populate-cache? to the closed raw relationship request keys, implemented in the Jank client boundary.
The Jank port inlines relay and continuation behavior; target lineage and proof-equivalent cursor paths remain to compare.

Every applicable locked-context change is specialized and executable-tested: the context owns the selected borrowed basis, validates and exposes its complete semantic identity and lineage, releases construction failures and successful requests exactly once, and binds cross-request plans to store/lifecycle/certified schema generation. Completed-answer proofs add relation stamps and a selected-basis ordering guard, so newer artifacts cannot answer older exact snapshots. Generic proof-frame objects, multi-adapter derived registries, owned native handles, and owner-thread snapshot policies are not linked in the closed single-memory-adapter, borrowed-any-thread source topology.
The target change only narrows a JVM/CLJS startup warning string; the Jank runtime always supplies an explicit keyring.
The mixed-arrow-target error carries the target Core eacl/error identity in the vendored parser.

The complete target delta is mapped to the specialized split cache: read-only cache requests retain lookup and request-local false/nil memoization while suppressing completed-answer publication; reusable plan/proof state names and keys certified schema generation; and corresponding local-cache configuration failures carry matching type/eacl-error identities. The target's generic weighted multi-tier store and managed projection abstraction are not linked by this closed port and were unchanged behaviors rather than rebase additions.

The changed generated-kernel boundary is not linked into the native runtime: its exact-integer relocation has no exposed generic host-number boundary, while its cache and continuation decisions are implemented and gated in the specialized production cache/cursor entries rather than by an unused Dafny selection wrapper.
